name: Alternate-day fasting

lead: Alternate-day fasting alternates fast days, with no or very few calories, with normal eating days. Followers use it for rapid fat loss and a leaner face and physique.

The fast days create a large weekly calorie deficit, and the body fat that comes off is what changes appearance. Randomized trials in adults with and without obesity report meaningful weight loss, generally comparable to daily calorie restriction; appearance itself was not the outcome measured.

paras: The strict form uses no calories on fast days; the modified form allows roughly a quarter of usual energy needs, often 0 to 500 kcal. Fast days alternate with unrestricted days. People often continue for weeks to months, tracking weight.
Hunger, irritability, headaches and low energy are reported early on. It is advised against in pregnancy, for young people, underweight people and anyone with an eating-disorder history.

angle.text: Followers use alternate-day fasting to lose fat fast and get a leaner face and physique. The fast days create a large weekly calorie deficit; trials show weight loss comparable to ordinary calorie restriction.

lead: Alternate-day fasting (ADF) is an intermittent fasting pattern in which fast days alternate with unrestricted "feast" days. In the strict form no calories are eaten on fast days; in the modified form roughly a quarter of usual energy needs, often 0 to 500 kcal, is allowed.[1][2]

It is used for weight and fat loss and is discussed in appearance communities as a route to leanness. Randomized trials in adults with obesity and in healthy non-obese people have compared it with daily calorie restriction or normal eating.[3][4][5]
Reviews describe the evidence as preliminary: weight loss is clinically meaningful but generally not greater than with continuous calorie restriction.[1][2]

paras: Alternate-day fasting is one of the most studied forms of intermittent fasting, alongside the 5:2 diet and time-restricted eating.[2] Fasting for obesity treatment has been studied since at least 1915, with renewed medical interest in the 1960s.[1]

A 2022 review in Nature Reviews Endocrinology states that intermittent fasting diets can produce clinically significant weight loss.[2] Wikipedia summarises most human studies as showing weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent, mostly fat, with some lean mass lost, and limited evidence of superiority over continuous calorie restriction.[1]
A one-year randomized trial in adults with obesity compared ADF with daily calorie restriction for weight loss, weight maintenance and cardiovascular risk indicators.[3]

Reported short-term effects of intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, typically fading within about a month.[1] A trial of strict ADF in healthy middle-aged people reported no adverse effects, including at follow-up beyond six months.[4]
Intermittent fasting is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and adolescents, underweight people and those with or at risk of eating disorders.[1]
A 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine randomized trial compared ADF with daily calorie restriction in metabolically healthy adults with obesity.[3]

A 2019 randomized trial in healthy non-obese adults found that four weeks of strict ADF, with an average 37 percent calorie reduction, improved markers of general health including cardiovascular markers.[4]

Earlier trials examined ADF in normal-weight and overweight people, in nonobese subjects, in obese adults combined with endurance exercise, and zero-calorie ADF versus daily restriction.[5][6][7][8][9]
A 2015 review examined intermittent fasting effects on body composition and clinical health markers.[10]
In a 2003 study, mice on an alternate-day regimen showed improved glucose metabolism and neuronal resistance to injury without a reduction in overall food intake.[11]

timeline.event: Fasting for obesity is described in the medical literature.[1]
